notes:
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the rest of the controls are along the bottom again, the way they were in version 24.

The previous release put them in a rail down the right-hand edge. The reasoning was that this is a right-hand-drive truck, so the right edge is the near edge for the driver - but where a control lives is the driver's call, not an argument about geometry, and the bottom is where they were wanted.

The bar carries six items: Home, Apps, Overlays, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and Settings, all at a size meant to be hit while moving. Only the item you are on is labelled. The bar this descends from had eight items with labels small enough to be unreadable at arm's length, and going to no labels at all would leave Overlays impossible to guess, so one label - always the one you are on - teaches the set by use.

The small coloured marker survives, turned on its side: a short ice-blue line above whatever you are on, sliding across as you move between screens. Home is a real destination on the bar now, so that marker always has somewhere to rest and always means "you are here".

Settings uses the same bar, so the two screens cannot drift apart again. Its section tabs keep the same sliding marker but draw it in white rather than blue, because the bottom bar owns the one coloured element on any screen and two blue lines would be two things both claiming to be the important one.

The bar costs the live panes about ninety points of height and hands back the ninety-six the rail was taking in width. Live content is usually wider than it is tall, so that comes out close to even and the panes have barely changed size.

Also in this build: the bottom row is rebalanced. With three launchable apps on this head unit the shortcuts card was mostly empty space, while the music card had too little room to show a song title once artwork and the transport buttons were in it. Music now gets the wider share, and the track name is readable.

Nine rendered views of the cockpit and settings are stored in the repository, and any future change that disturbs them fails the build.

Still to check in the truck, unchanged from the last release: whether a window can be parked off-screen when a pane is swiped away from an app, and whether the divider between two panes can be grabbed in the gap between two windows.
